chunk_findings.detail: `_guard` is documented/annotated as catching "a config that does not load" (`except ValueError as exc: # a config that does not load`), but the handler is wrapped around the *entire* body `fn()`, not around the `_load`/`Config.load` call. As a result, every `ValueError` raised anywhere in the operation is silently relabeled as an unreadable config and returned with exit `EXIT_UNAVAILABLE` and the message `f"could not read the config: {exc}"`. This misfires for the very operations this task adds. For example, `export_validate` is specified to "report template errors with file and line" and to "exit 2 when any template does not render"; if the template layer surfaces a `ValueError` (a renderer that raises `ValueError("template <path> line N: ...")` rather than returning a `results` entry, or any `ValueError` out of `ops.selection`/`T.validate`), the guard converts it into `EXIT_UNAVAILABLE` with the misleading "could not read the config" text instead of exit 2 with the template's file/line. Likewise an invalid selection/mode that `S.enable`/`S.disable` rejects via `ValueError` is reported to the operator (and over MCP) as a config-read failure rather than as a usage error. The config-load mapping should be scoped to the `_load(repo, …)`/`Config.load(repo)` call (or use a dedicated config exception), so that `ValueError`s originating in the operation are not swallowed and misattributed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/export.py:_guard (the `except ValueError` arm)

chunk_findings.detail: The reducer clears the operator veto unconditionally, but its own comment asserts an invariant it never checks: `"locked": False,  # only a person at a terminal can enable a locked document`. Nothing in the handler looks at `prev.get("locked")` or at `human`; any `export.enabled` event — including one whose `data.human` is false/absent (i.e. an agent-authored event, an MCP-emitted event from a client that doesn't run the CLI's lock check, or an event replayed from a newer/foreign log, which the intent explicitly enables via "optional event kinds ... forward-compat B1c4a2346a9") — silently rewrites `st.exports[doc]` with `locked: False`. Concretely: with state `exports["brief"] = {..., "enabled": False, "locked": True}` produced by `disable brief --lock`, replaying `{"kind": "export.enabled", "subject": "brief", "agent": "claude", "data": {"path": "docs/brief.md", "mode": "whole"}}` yields `exports["brief"]["locked"] == False` and `enabled == True`. The veto is then permanently gone (nothing else in this hunk ever restores `locked`), so the very next agent `export enable brief` no longer exits 3 and the doctor/brief no longer report the lock. The handler should preserve an existing lock unless the enabling actor is human (`locked = prev_locked and not human`), instead of trusting the writer to have enforced it — note that the sibling `_h_export_disabled` does defend its side of the invariant with `bool(prev.get("locked")) or bool(d.get("locked"))`, showing the gate is expected to live in the model, not only in the caller.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/model.py `_h_export_enabled`

chunk_findings.detail:
The disabled event stores the *value of the `--lock` argument* rather than the lock state that results from the call. The lock is not stored in the config; it lives only in state derived from these events (`_locked` reads `st.exports[doc]["locked"]`, and the `enable` event relies on the very same value-assignment semantics — its `"locked": False` is what lifts the operator's lock). Therefore *any* `export.disabled` record carrying `"locked": false` overwrites a prior `"locked": true`, i.e. a plain, unprivileged `disable` clears the operator's veto.

Concrete failure: doc `x` is listed by a config layer the write does not touch (e.g. `[export].documents` only in the local layer, or a union-merged layer). The operator runs `ddflow export disable x --lock` (without `--local`): `was` is true so the doc is "removed" from a layer that does not contain it, the code itself warns `"x is still selected: another config layer sets [export].documents (try with --local)"`, and the appended event leaves x selected-in-config but `locked=True, enabled=False`. An agent now runs `ddflow export disable x` (allowed — only `lock and why_agent` is refused): `was` is still true, so a new `export.disabled` event with `"locked": false` is appended and the lock silently disappears. A subsequent agent `ddflow export enable x` no longer reaches the lock branch of `enable` and exits 0 where the decision requires exit 3, even though unlocking is supposed to be operator-only. Recording `"locked": lock or already_locked` (or leaving the existing lock untouched for a non-locking disable) would preserve the veto.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/select.py:disable — the `log.append("export.disabled", doc, {... "locked": lock})` payload

chunk_findings.detail: The code that renders each row is written defensively for the optional "locked"/enable annotations — `r.get("locked")` and `r.get("enabled_by")` — but then reads the companion enable fields with hard indexing: `str(r['enabled_at'])`, `r["acknowledged"]` and `r["by_agent"]` (all three inside the `if r.get("enabled_by"):` block). That tolerance is precisely what the forward-compat requirement (B1c4a2346a9) implies: enable records may come from payloads that carry `enabled_by` but not the newer `acknowledged`/`by_agent` fields (e.g. a record written by an older/partial producer, or an enable whose ack state is not materialised in the row). Given such a row, `r["acknowledged"]` (or `r["by_agent"]`) raises `KeyError` while the list is being printed, so `ddflow export` crashes instead of listing, whereas the sibling keys are handled via `.get`. Use `r.get("acknowledged")` / `r.get("by_agent")` / `r.get("enabled_at")` (defaulting appropriately) to match the rest of the block.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/export.py:_list (the `state` rendering block)

chunk_findings.detail: The help text states "The events are `export.enabled`, `export.disabled`, `export.acknowledged`", presenting three event kinds as the set emitted by enable/disable/ack. The stated intent for this change defines exactly two: "export.enabled / export.disabled optional event kinds (core/model.py; forward-compat B1c4a2346a9) with agent, document, path, mode, time, locked". No `export.acknowledged` kind is defined, and its field set (agent, document, path, mode, time, locked) is not specified for it, so a consumer that subscribes to `export.acknowledged` (e.g. to detect that the operator has seen agent-enabled documents) would wait for an event that the implementation never emits, or would be relying on an unregistered kind. The ack action only changes local brief/doctor state per the spec ("brief line until acknowledged (`ddflow export` at a TTY or `export ack`)"); the documentation should not advertise a third event kind.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/prompts/help/export.md:63

chunk_findings.detail: `export_ack` calls `S.acknowledge(log, st, cfg, requested_agent=agent)`, i.e. it passes `log, state, config` — while every other caller in this module (`S.enable`, `S.disable`) passes `repo, log, cfg, st, doc, ...`. If `S.acknowledge` follows the same `(..., log, cfg, st, ...)` convention as its siblings, then `st` is bound to the `cfg` parameter and `cfg` to the state parameter. Running `ddflow export ack` after an agent has enabled a document then either crashes (an `AttributeError`/`TypeError` is *not* caught by `_guard`, which only handles `ExportError` and `ValueError`, so the user sees a traceback) or silently acknowledges against the wrong object, so the brief line never clears. Either way the state/config arguments are transposed relative to the rest of this file.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/export.py:export_ack

chunk_findings.detail: `_guard` catches `except ValueError` and unconditionally reports `f"could not read the config: {exc}"` with `EXIT_UNAVAILABLE`, but it wraps the *entire* body of every command, not just the config load. `run()` calls `R.get(doc)`, `ops.selection(cfg)`, `S.enable/S.disable` (which validate `mode`/`path`), `T.validate`, and `ops.worst([r["code"] for r in bad])`. Any `ValueError` originating in those (e.g. an unknown document name from `R.get`, an invalid `--mode`, or an `ops.worst([])`/`max([])` on the all-templates-render happy path of `export validate`) is mislabeled as an unreadable config and given the config-unavailable exit code instead of the domain error the user actually made. Concretely, `ddflow export enable <doc> --mode bogus` (or `ddflow export validate`) reports "could not read the config: ..." rather than a usage/validation error, and the same exit code is shared with the `disable --lock` veto, making the two indistinguishable to callers.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/export.py:_guard

chunk_findings.detail:
`disable` computes `already_locked` but never uses it in the event payload; it writes `"locked": lock`, i.e. `False` for any call without `--lock`. The guard `if was or (lock and not already_locked)` only protects the case where the document is *not* in the effective selection. When a locked document is still effectively selected (exactly the "another config layer sets [export].documents" situation the function itself warns about — e.g. the doc is listed in both a global and a local layer), an agent can drop the operator's veto:

1. Operator: `ddflow export disable D --lock`. The write removes D from one layer, but D is still in the effective selection via the other layer; the event records `locked: True`.
2. Agent (MCP, or DDFLOW_AGENT/CLAUDECODE, or `--agent`): `ddflow export disable D` (no `--lock`). `was` is `True` (D is still selected), so the branch is taken and the event records `{"human": False, "locked": False}`. Both on a merge-style state model and on a replace-style one, `st.exports["D"]["locked"]` becomes `False`.
3. The follow-up agent `ddflow export enable D --path P --mode region` now sees `_locked(...) is None`, so it is no longer refused with exit 3 and rewrites the locked document's path/mode.

Expected: the operator's lock should survive a plain (non-`--lock`) disable until a human enables the document again. The payload should be `"locked": lock or already_locked` (or the event should be skipped when `already_locked` and the caller is not re-locking).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/select.py :: disable (`log.append("export.disabled", ..., "locked": lock)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new enable/ack annotation block is guarded only on `r.get("enabled_by")`, but then reads three sibling keys with direct subscripting: `r['enabled_at']`, `r['acknowledged']`, and `r['by_agent']`. The asymmetry is the tell — the author defensively uses `.get()` for `enabled_by` and `locked` (the keys that may or may not be present), yet assumes the other three are always co-present whenever `enabled_by` is truthy. A row that carries an enabler identity but no acknowledgement metadata therefore aborts the entire listing with `KeyError` rather than printing it. Concretely, the operator-side enable path records an enabler (so `enabled_by` is a non-empty string such as the operator/user name) while acknowledgement fields (`acknowledged`, `by_agent`) are attributes of *agent* enables and are absent from that row; running `ddflow export` (or `ddflow export --json`? no, the text branch) then crashes inside the `for r in rows` loop before any line is printed, so a single operator-enabled document makes the whole list unusable. Reading these three via `r.get(...)` (with sensible defaults) is required for the same reason the author already used `.get` on `enabled_by`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/export.py:_list

chunk_findings.detail: `cmd_export` routes every invocation that has no document and no `--all` to `_list` (`if not a.doc and not a.all: return _list(c)`), and `_list` is also the routine that implements the other no-document modes (`--check`, `--out`, `--diff`). The new block at the tail of that routine runs `A.export_ack(...)` whenever `pending` is non-empty and both stdio streams are TTYs, with no check of which mode the user actually asked for. Concrete case: with one unacknowledged agent enable on disk, an operator at a terminal runs `ddflow export --out <dir>` (or `ddflow export --check`) — a read-only/export command, not the listing — and the routine writes the config and clears the unacknowledged markers (exit 0). Afterwards the brief no longer appears on `ddflow export` for anyone (the ack is repo-global), even though nobody ran the listing that the spec ties the acknowledgment to ("`ddflow export` at a TTY or `export ack`"). The ack should be gated on the plain-listing mode (e.g. no `--check`/`--out`/`--diff`/`--update`), or only performed from `export ack`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/export.py:_list (new `pending` / `A.export_ack` block)

chunk_findings.detail: The verb test is applied to the same positional that carries the document name for the ordinary select/print path, and `_verb` then reads the verb's document from the second positional `a.target`. A document whose name is a verb is therefore shadowed: given a document named `ack` (or `enable`/`disable`/`eject`/`validate`), `ddflow export ack` no longer selects/prints that document but instead runs the `ack` verb (clearing pending markers) and exits 0, and there is no syntax left to reach the `ack` document at all (the doc must be supplied as the *target* of a verb, which `ack`/`validate` ignore). Either the verb must come from a dedicated positional/flag distinct from the document argument, or verb-named documents must be explicitly rejected rather than silently re-dispatched to a state-mutating command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/export.py:cmd_export (`if a.doc in VERBS`)

chunk_findings.detail: The added parity entry classifies `--lock` as operator-only, but the intent states only *unlocking* is operator-only (“unlocking is operator-only (refused under --agent/DDFLOW_AGENT/CLAUDECODE…”). Locking via `disable --lock` is therefore available to agents, and the MCP `ddflow_export` disable action should expose a `lock` argument. With this entry the parity test will either fail if the MCP schema correctly adds `lock`, or it will permanently forbid agent locking, contradicting the intended behavior.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new guard `"locked": bool(st.exports.get(ev.subject, {}).get("locked")) and not human` makes the event's own `human` bit the *only* evidence that a person — rather than an event writer — lifted the operator's veto. But `fold` is handed nothing except the event list, so `human` is attacker/foreign-controlled data by construction. A forged `export.enabled` event can therefore still clear the lock by simply setting `human=True`; the comment ("the fold does not trust a forged or foreign event to have") does not hold. Concretely, using the same event shape as the new test but flipping one field:

    model.fold([
        _ev("export.disabled", "roadmap", 1, by="op", human=True, locked=True),
        _ev("export.enabled",  "roadmap", 2, by="bot", human=True),   # forged human bit
    ])["roadmap"]["locked"]  # -> False

yields `False`, i.e. the operator's veto is lifted by an event authored by an agent. The new test only covers the forgery that omits `human`, so the stated security property ("agent enable does not lift the operator's lock") is exercised in exactly the case where the raw `locked` field was ignored, not where the trusted bit is spoofed. If the fold is meant to be the backstop against forged/foreign events (as the comment claims), it cannot derive `human` from the same untrusted payload it is trying to validate.
